source.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
source.authors: Cheng-Yu Xie; Fei Shen; Shu-Yi Miao; Yue Feng; Jian Yu; Pengyang Shao; Yi-Jun Tian; Xiao-Yu Du

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, though it contains some layout and template artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether a compact set of internal coordinates is functionally associated with safety, using activation masking and transfer rather than the claim's fine-tuning, KL-position, or opening-token tests.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on localized neuron interventions and their safety outcomes. It does not test harmful or benign fine-tuning that erodes safety, per-token KL concentration, compliant-prefix or suffix bypasses, or training to deepen safety. Results comparing SK-Masked LoRA with other training methods are not evidence that pre-existing safety is carried by a small parameter set.
record.test_reason: The study zeroes a small set of FFN output coordinates (0.12–0.15% of analyzed coordinates) in instruction-tuned models and reports MultiJail ASR against size- and module-matched random masks. This directly tests whether a small set of units carries safety behaviour (V5). Zeroing an FFN output coordinate is equivalent to ablating the corresponding weight row. The method (SCAR selection plus activation masking) differs from the original sources' approach, so the tranche is T2. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that a compact cross-lingual intersection of FFN neurons (the safety kernel) is functionally associated with multilingual safety: suppressing it raises ASR, and injecting a safe-refusal state through it lowers ASR. They also conclude that SK-Masked LoRA reduces ASR across models, benchmarks and held-out languages with limited capability change.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SCAR-based cross-language neuron selection, activation suppression and state transfer, and SK-masked LoRA; it does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL or test shallow-token bypasses.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports language-specific differences in masking outcomes, activation-transfer improvement magnitude varying by model, and a top-k suppression effect that stabilizes around k = 5000 for English.
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates or significance tests are stated for the reported ASR values. The activation-transfer averages are reported in text, while per-language values appear only in Figure 3. Activation interventions establish a role for neuron coordinates but do not directly test whether weights or ranks carry safety.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant intervention outcomes were left out. Table 3 and Table 4 fine-tuning/evaluation results and Table 5 update-scope comparisons were not recorded as V5 evidence because safety was deliberately trained into the model, so those outcomes do not show that pre-existing safety is carried by a small set of parameters.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning of aligned models.
No benign fine-tuning measured for safety erosion.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks; cross-lingual prompts are used only as the evaluation set.

Low-rank/rank-level localization and direct weight ablation were not tested. General capability under SK masking (whether masking specifically removes safety or degrades the model broadly) was not reported; MMLU/MGSM are reported only for the LoRA variants.
No test of what produces shallowness.
SK-Masked LoRA is safety fine-tuning, but it is not evaluated for depth beyond the first tokens or for robustness to attack or fine-tuning.

missing.what: Top-k sweep: ASR increase after masking as k varies 2000–7000 for English on both models. It shows how large the set must be for the effect to stabilize (~k=5000), which bears on how small the safety-carrying set is.
Per-language activation-transfer ASR (KO, TH, BN) before and after injection for each model, including Llama KO and BN values in the 36–43% range.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The record's limits_scope label on the random-control rows was wrong: matched controls staying near default support V5's specificity, so the averaged controls are moved into the supports group. Only the per-language control anomalies (Llama KO, BN) limit scope. Evidence is activation masking of FFN output coordinates applied at all positions. ASR is judged by GPT-4o only, with no uncertainty or significance reported. Capability under masking is not reported, so masking could also degrade general behaviour. Tables 3–5 (SK-Masked LoRA vs baselines and update-scope ablations) train safety in and are correctly excluded as V5 evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning examples cause harmful compliance.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning data raises harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as refusal bypasses.
The study intervenes on FFN activation coordinates, not direct weight ablations or ranks.
Whether data or a training objective produces first-token shallowness.
Training safety beyond the first tokens and evaluating whether that deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-it, MultiJail, SK (0.12–0.15% of FFN coordinates) and language-wise top-5000 (~0.55%) sets masked at inference
relationships.reason: SK masking raises average ASR by 52.65 and 45.13 points, while matched random masks change it by +1.17 and −2.33 (t2-qwen-sk, t2-llama-sk vs t2-qwen-random, t2-llama-random). Language-wise masks raise ASR to ~70–81% in every language (t1-qwen-*, t1-llama-en…th).
relationships.display_finding: Masking the kernel raised average attack success by 52.65 and 45.13 points, while matched random masks changed it by +1.17 and −2.33. Language-wise masks raised attack success to about 70–81% in every language.

relation.reason: The study directly measures changes in harmful compliance after interventions on a compact set of FFN coordinates.

tranche.reason: SCAR-selected activation suppression and state transfer test sparse safety localization through a different method.

source_check.notes: The percentages describe analyzed FFN output activation coordinates, not fractions of model weights or ranks. Capability checks concern LoRA adaptation; capability preservation under activation suppression is unmeasured.

statements.correction: Llama-3.1-8B-it random masking: KO 30.47→40.95%; BN 65.71→46.03%. SK state transfer at alpha=4 over KO/TH/BN: Qwen3-8B 20.21→11.96%; Llama-3.1-8B-it 35.98→30.69%; Gemma-2-9B-it 5.18→3.17%. Transfer supports safety modulation through the selected coordinates.
statements.problem: The descriptive findings are correct, but incomplete safe-state transfer alone does not limit V5, which does not predict complete safety restoration.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Selected language-wise neuron coordinates and the cross-lingual SK on the tested models and MultiJail settings
reader_labels.reason: Masking selected coordinates substantially raises ASR, while the much smaller SK also causes a large rise; the cited outcomes are in rows t1-qwen-en through t1-llama-bn and t2-qwen-sk.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports random-mask ASR as close to default overall, though a few language-specific control values move appreciably; this supports specificity of the selected coordinates rather than an effect of arbitrary small sets.
